Consult Summary:
- 31-year-old with 4-day history of intensely pruritic, sore, red rash (chest, hands, inside elbows) with cracked skin and sleep/work impairment; past eczema; no systemic symptoms; clinician assessed likely eczema flare; prescribed stronger topical steroid, emollients, and fexofenadine; advised trigger diary and follow-up if not improving in 1 week.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Very itchy, sore, red skin rash; cracked areas; significantly disrupts sleep and concentration at work; hiking worsened pain; showers provide temporary relief.
- Timeline: Onset 4 days ago; persistent. More itchy and more widespread than prior eczema (previously mainly arms).
- Distribution: Chest, hands, inside elbows; denies face and legs. Conflict noted: clinician later stated “mainly chest and back” (see Quality checks).
- Prior treatments: Past eczema controlled with prescribed cream and shower product. Current episode: tried OTC “steroid cream” last night without relief; tried antihistamines recently without relief.
- Associated symptoms: Denies fever/temperature. No cough or breathing difficulties. Bowels and urination normal.
- Triggers/exposures: No known changes to shower gel or clothing; no clear trigger identified.

Past Medical History:
- Eczema (prior diagnosis; previously responsive to topical therapy/shower additive; current flare reported).
- Asthma in the past; not currently active.
- No other conditions reported.

Medications:
- Regular: None reported.
- Recent/OTC: “Steroid cream” from pharmacy (name/dose/route/frequency not documented). Antihistamines tried recently (names/doses not documented) with no benefit.
- Prescribed today:
  - Stronger topical steroid (name/dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Emollients for bathing/showering and moisturizing (product and instructions not documented).
  - Fexofenadine (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Counseling: May try OTC loratadine or Piriton for itch.

Allergies:
- No known allergies.

Social History:
- Lives with flatmates; full-time project manager at a pharmaceutical company.
- Non-smoker.
- Alcohol: A few beers per week; drank more when younger.
- Hobbies: Hiking (limited by current symptoms).

Family History:
- Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not documented.
- Skin: Patient reports dry, cracked areas. Clinician noted on inspection that rash “appears familiar.” No further objective findings documented.

Investigations:
- None ordered or reported.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Likely eczema flare (pruritic, erythematous, sore rash; 4-day duration; cracked skin; prior eczema; no systemic signs).
  - Prescribe higher-potency topical steroid (details not documented).
  - Prescribe and use emollients regularly, including in bath/shower; assess effect after 7–10 days.
  - Trial fexofenadine (details not documented); OTC options (loratadine or Piriton) discussed.
  - Keep a diary of potential triggers (soaps, shower gels, clothing, exposures).
  - Follow-up: Return in 1 week if not improved; earlier if worsening or signs of infection (pus, spreading redness, fever).

- General Plan items:
  - Education on regular moisturization and avoidance of potential irritants.
  - Clinician mentioned possible discussion about an “eczema CU” (meaning unclear in transcript).

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements:
  - Vitals not recorded.
  - Detailed skin exam description (morphology, extent, photos) not documented.
  - Exact drug names, potencies, doses, route, and frequency for prescribed steroid, emollient regimen, and fexofenadine not documented.
  - Name of OTC steroid cream and specific antihistamines previously used not documented.
  - Family history and immunization status not obtained.
- Internal conflicts:
  - Distribution: Patient reported chest, hands, and inside elbows; denied face and legs. Clinician later referenced chest and back. Conflict noted.
  - Duration referenced as 3 vs 4 days; patient confirmed 4 days.
  - Patient addressed as “sir,” later called “Sarah” (likely audio/name confusion).
- Transcript quality: Intermittent audio issues and dropouts; some phrases unclear (e.g., “eczema CU”).
